text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers.
- Jobs are the top issue in Sunday's European parliamentary elections. Only around ten percent believe a bigger role for the far-right Freedom Party would be a very good thing, a study says.

- Transport Minister Rudolf Scholten has signed a contract with China's railways minister covering an order with engineer Siemens Austria's unit SGP-Verkehrtechnik. The order is for twenty locomotives worth one billion schillings.

- Klaus Liebscher, president of Austria's central bank expects Italy, Austria's second most important trading partner, to join European Monetary Union by the year 2000 at the latest. He noted that the Italian government is planning an ambitious restructuring programme.
- The European Commission's final opinion on Austria's anonymous savings accounts will be presented after Sunday's European parliamentary elections in Austria.
- Fiscal policies of European Union members is slowing down economic growth. However LINK, an international group of economic experts, is optimistic for the further development of Europe's economy.
- Sugar and flour maker Agrana is interested in taking over Austria's former salt monopoly Salinen AG.
- Social Minister Franz Hums wants Austrians to retire later and give them more opportunity to take off work time for recreation and education.
- Workers at German tyre maker Continental's Austrian unit will probably not start a strike against plans to move parts of the production facilties to the Czech Republic.
- Austria's economy is more dynamic than Switzerland's due to its membership of the European Union, a finance ministry spokesman said.

- Vienna airport is taking legal action against the state claiming the government has failed to cover expenses incurred under the European Union's Schengen agreement. The government had agreed to make some payments to the firm.
- An economist at Vienna-based Wifo said the state should only provide a basic pension. He warns that otherwise there will be chaos in Austria's pension system.
- Interest rates will rise after the introduction of a single European currency, said Investkredit boss Alfred Reiter.
- Steyr in Austria, Munich in Germany and Tunbridge in Britain are fighting for a big investment by BMW in a planned new production plant. A decision is expected by the end of October.
